top_level_objectives: Explain apparent retrograde motion from Earth's perspective.
Explain apparent retrograde motion from an external, heliocentric perspective.
Compare the retrograde motion of different outer planets (Mars, Jupiter, Saturn).
Relate apparent retrograde motion to the historical shift from geocentric to heliocentric models.

scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce the phenomenon of apparent retrograde motion as observed from Earth.
key_visuals: Night sky view centered on Mars
student_actions: Observe Mars's position against the background stars over several simulated weeks.
Note the general eastward drift of Mars.

scenes.brief_purpose: Illustrate the period when Mars appears to reverse its direction.
key_visuals: Night sky view centered on Mars
student_actions: Observe Mars's position over several simulated weeks, focusing on the period of westward motion.
Identify the start and end points of the retrograde loop.

scenes.brief_purpose: Show Mars returning to its normal eastward motion after the retrograde loop.
key_visuals: Night sky view centered on Mars
student_actions: Observe Mars's position over several simulated weeks after the loop.
Confirm that Mars's eastward motion has resumed.

scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce the heliocentric model and the orbits of Earth and Mars.
key_visuals: Concentric circular orbits for Earth and Mars
Earth's orbit shown as inner and faster than Mars's outer orbit
student_actions: Observe the Sun, Earth, and Mars in their orbital paths.
Note that Earth orbits closer to the Sun and completes its orbit faster than Mars.

scenes.brief_purpose: Demonstrate how Earth's faster orbital speed causes the apparent retrograde motion of Mars.
key_visuals: Sun, Earth, and Mars in orbit
Earth overtaking Mars on its inner orbit
Lines of sight from Earth to Mars during the overtaking
student_actions: Play the animation of Earth and Mars orbiting the Sun.
Relate this overtaking motion to the retrograde loop seen from Earth's surface.

scenes.brief_purpose: Compare the retrograde motion of Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.
key_visuals: Sun, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn in orbit
Simulated sky views showing retrograde loops for each planet
student_actions: Observe the orbits of Jupiter and Saturn relative to Earth and Mars.
Compare the duration and apparent 'size' of the retrograde loops for Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.
Infer why the effect is less pronounced for planets farther from the Sun.
